findings.text: The Factory Licence process flows through five stages: online application, multi-level departmental scrutiny, deficiency/correction handling, physical inspection, and licence issuance; the official's account did not describe a separate fee-payment step.
Officials acknowledged delays in communicating identified deficiencies or discrepancies back to applicants, requiring them to submit additional documents or corrections.
Portal downtime was cited by the official as having affected application submission and processing, despite the process being largely digitised.
The factory building/layout plan must be resubmitted at every licence renewal even when there has been no change to the layout or infrastructure.
Officials recommended requiring only revised/modified factory plans at renewal when alterations have actually been made, with previously approved plans otherwise continuing to be valid.

An approval timeline of around 65 days was discussed and characterised by the official as lengthy from the applicant's perspective; the exact governing Act/Rule and a separate average actual timeline were not specified.
Officials stated that risk-based classification is not readily applicable to Factory Licence approvals, limiting scope for differentiated treatment of lower-risk establishments.

Official recommendations included timely communication of application status and deficiencies, improving portal stability/reliability, strengthening single-window integration, and examining best practices from other Indian states or abroad.
Applicants reported little or no communication from the department after submitting applications, often remaining unaware of pending deficiencies until contacted after a considerable delay.
Applications frequently remain pending due to document verification, scrutiny, and administrative processing, resulting in longer approval timelines.
Applicants indicated insufficient guidance on documentation requirements and procedural steps, noting there is no SOP or process flow published on the official website.
Participants experienced difficulty reaching concerned departmental officials for clarification or updates, further delaying resolution of application-related issues.

Factory Licence validity is only 1 year, which participants said creates a recurring compliance and renewal burden; they suggested longer validity or a permanent licence with annual fee payment instead.
There is no formal policy requiring the department to proactively communicate application status, deficiencies, or required actions to applicants, leading to prolonged uncertainty.

While applications are submitted online, participants felt the existing framework does not ensure end-to-end digital processing or transparent tracking, forcing applicants to visit the department office regularly to track verification.
Minor discrepancies identified during scrutiny or verification often trigger repeated resubmission of the same supporting documents.
One participant reported waiting three to four months, with the process only moving forward after a departmental officer personally contacted them to request the required documents.

Participants suggested extending licence validity or introducing a permanent licence with annual fee payment, explicitly citing Trade Licence's move to automatic renewal after payment as a model to follow.
For small units, participants proposed introducing self-certification instead of extensive inspections.
Participants acknowledged that the online application system has improved accessibility compared to the earlier manual process, though further enhancements are needed.

The portal, unnamed in the ED, is identified by secondary research as SilpaSathi (silpasathi.wb.gov.in), made the exclusive mandatory channel for Factory Licence from 1 January 2023 per a December 2022 Labour Department notification.

SilpaSathi's own official user manual states a 65-day WBRTPS timeline for a fresh licence, independently confirming the official's ~65-day figure with a citable source rather than just his self-characterisation of it as lengthy.

No deemed-approval-to-applicant clause was found anywhere in the WB Right to Public Services Act framework for Factory Licence; only a penalty on the delaying officer (Rs 250-1,000 fine) exists, with no automatic grant to the applicant.

Fees are set under Schedules A, B, C of the West Bengal Factories Rules, calculated by the Inspector of Factories, and paid via treasury receipt, due annually before 31 December along with a Form 2 renewal return -- though exact rupee figures could not be found.

A separate 2017 RTPS gazette sets a longer 90-day timeline specifically for renewal/amendment/transfer, distinct from the 65-day timeline that applies to a fresh grant -- a distinction not mentioned in either the ED or the FGD.

gaps.text: Portal identity: the ED does not name the portal used for Factory Licence. Secondary research identifies it as SilpaSathi (silpasathi.wb.gov.in), made the exclusive mandatory channel from 1 January 2023 per a December 2022 Labour Department notification, replacing an earlier standalone departmental system.

Timeline: the ED's ~65-day figure was only the official's own self-characterisation ('lengthy'), with no governing Act/Rule cited. Secondary research found SilpaSathi's own official user manual independently states a 65-day WBRTPS timeline for a fresh licence, and also surfaced a separate 90-day timeline (2017 RTPS gazette) specifically for renewal/amendment/transfer -- a distinction neither the ED nor FGD mentioned.

Deemed approval: the ED explicitly states this was unclear/not identified, and the FGD does not mention deemed approval at all. Secondary research found no deemed-approval-to-applicant clause anywhere in the WB Right to Public Services Act framework -- only a Rs 250-1,000 fine on the delaying officer, with no automatic grant to the applicant. This confirms the FGD's real-world account (an uncushioned 3-4 month wait, no safeguard ever invoked) over any assumption of an unstated mechanism.

Exact statutory/application fee amount: the ED states no fee figure or variation by establishment size/employees/validity was given, and the FGD gives no INR figures at all. Secondary research found the fee basis (Schedules A, B, C of the WB Factories Rules; calculated by the Inspector of Factories; paid via treasury receipt; due annually before 31 December with a Form 2 renewal return) but could not locate the actual rupee amounts -- this gap remains open even after the web-search pass.

Validity period for the initial (first-grant) licence is not stated in the ED at all. Only the FGD gives a figure -- 'validity of the license is only 1 year' -- which is not itself traced to a specific statute or rule in either transcript, though it is structurally consistent with secondary research's finding of an annual (before 31 December) renewal cycle.

ED frames the process as largely digitised/online, with portal downtime as the main technical complaint ('The Factory Licence process is largely digitised/online... portal downtime has affected application submission and processing'). FGD participants go further and directly contest the 'effectively digital' framing: they state the digital system provides no real-time tracking, no proactive communication, and no automated notifications, forcing applicants to 'visit the department office regularly to track the verification process' and, in one cited case, to simply wait 3-4 months until an officer personally made contact.

Both ED and FGD independently converge on the same concrete fix: stop requiring resubmission of the factory building/layout plan (or other supporting documents) at every renewal when nothing has changed, and require revised plans/documents only when actual alterations have been made. The ED frames this as its main identified redundant requirement; the FGD's 'redundant/duplicate documents' theme describes the same pattern (resubmission triggered by any deficiency found at scrutiny).

FGD participants pointed to West Bengal's own Trade Licence scheme, which has moved to automatic renewal after payment ('Trade Licence has become much simpler with automatic renewal after payment. A similar approach can be adopted for Factory Licence'), as an in-state model worth examining -- consistent with the ED's own recommendation to 'examine and adopt relevant best practices from other Indian states or international jurisdictions.'
